name: Vedado
tagline: Leafy 1950s grid with the deepest supply of casas
description: Vedado is Havana's mid-century district, a numbered grid of shaded streets, faded modernist apartment blocks and grand porticoed houses running down to the Malecon seawall. It holds the greatest concentration of casas particulares with reliable rooms, plus the Hotel Nacional, cinemas, jazz clubs and paladares. Most long-stay visitors end up here.
bestFor: First-time long-stayers who want space, quiet nights and everything within a walk or a short taxi ride.
pros: Largest choice of casas and month-long rentals
Walkable flat grid with real neighbourhood shops
Best cluster of restaurants, bars and live music
cons: Rolling power cuts hit here like everywhere else
Street lighting is poor once the sun drops
Mobile data is the only realistic internet and it is slow

name: Habana Vieja
tagline: The restored colonial core, beautiful and busy
description: Old Havana is the UNESCO-listed colonial quarter of cobbled lanes, baroque churches and four restored plazas, wrapped around a still-crumbling residential centre. Boutique hotels, galleries and cafes with generators sit beside tenements with laundry over the balconies. It is the most photogenic base and by far the most touristed.
bestFor: Short stays where atmosphere and walkability matter more than value or peace.
pros: Everything is walkable, no transport needed
Most cafes with generators and paid wifi
Dense concentration of sights and museums
cons: Constant hustling and inflated tourist prices
Loud terraces and music until very late
Cramped rooms with weak natural light

name: Centro Habana
tagline: Raw, lived-in and the cheapest central option
description: Centro is the tight tenement grid between Old Havana and Vedado, where balconies sag over narrow streets, dominoes are played on the pavement and the Malecon is a short walk north. Rents are the lowest of any central district and daily life is entirely local, with peso markets and hole-in-the-wall pizza counters.
bestFor: Budget travellers who want to live among Habaneros rather than beside tour groups.
pros: Cheapest rooms within walking distance of the centre
Local peso prices for food and produce
Sits between Vedado and Old Havana
cons: Noisy, crowded and short on green space
Buildings are poorly maintained, water can cut out
Unlit streets warrant care after dark

name: Miramar
description: West of the tunnel, Miramar is Havana's diplomatic quarter: wide avenues lined with royal palms, walled 1940s mansions turned embassies, and a handful of business hotels. It is the calmest and greenest part of the city, with a few private clinics, supermarkets carrying imported goods and buildings that often have backup power.
bestFor: Remote workers who will pay more for calm, greenery and the steadiest power in the city.
pros: Quietest streets and most reliable electricity
Better stocked shops and private clinics
Seafront walks without the tourist crush
cons: Spread out, so you rely on taxis daily
Priced for diplomats, not for locals
Little street life or spontaneous nightlife

name: Nuevo Vedado
tagline: Residential hillside just south of the action
description: Nuevo Vedado climbs the slope south of Vedado proper, a mix of low-rise apartment blocks, single-family houses with gardens and the leafy edge of Bosque de La Habana. It is almost entirely residential, with the zoo, Colon cemetery and the Plaza de la Revolucion nearby, and rents noticeably below the Vedado grid.
bestFor: Stays of a month or more where a quiet desk and a garden beat being in the thick of it.
pros: Genuinely quiet, with gardens and trees
Ten to fifteen minutes by taxi to the centre
cons: Few restaurants or bars within walking distance
Hilly and spread out, transport needed
